entities.summary:
Louis de Bourbon, Prince du Sang and Cardinal of Vendôme (1493–1557), served as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in 16th-century France during the reigns of Francis I and Henry II. Born at Château de Ham, he was the second son of Francis, Count of Vendôme, and Marie of Luxembourg, placing him at the nexus of the French royal family and the high nobility. His career spanned the turbulent period of the Italian Wars and the nascent stages of the Reformation, where he leveraged his princely status and extensive ecclesiastical appointments to influence both church policy and dynastic affairs, particularly through his role as Archbishop of Sens and later as Papal Legate.

Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Leo X in 1517 at the age of 24, Louis de Bourbon accumulated a significant portfolio of benefices, including the Archbishopric of Sens (1525–1557) and the Bishoprics of Laon (1510–1552) and Luçon (1514–1524). Beyond his spiritual duties, he acted as a trusted royal advisor and diplomat, notably participating in the negotiations for the Treaty of Madrid in 1526, which aimed to secure the release of King Francis I from Habsburg captivity. His consistent presence in the French royal council underscored his influence in shaping foreign policy and mediating domestic political struggles, including those between the powerful Guise and Montmorency factions.
